notes: Instruction translates torah, teaching that directs life. Meditating can include murmuring or reciting it.
vocabulary: A sequence of involvement with the counsel, path, and company of the wicked.
Here knowing a way includes attentive concern for those who follow it.

sections.1: The nations and the LORD’s anointed

notes: The king reports a declaration of sonship. The psalm’s royal setting remains visible without adding a later doctrinal explanation.
The pointed Hebrew reads “break”; a different vocalization can give “shepherd.”

“Kiss the son” takes bar as the Aramaic word for son. The line is difficult; readings involving purity or homage expressed differently have also been proposed. The one whose anger burns is not explicitly renamed.
vocabulary: Someone consecrated with oil; here the king.

notes: The Hebrew title places the psalm during David’s flight from Absalom. It is translated before the poem inside public verse 1.
Striking the jaw and breaking teeth remain violent images of disabling enemies.
vocabulary: An ancient performance or musical marker whose precise meaning is uncertain.

notes: “Of David” can also mean “for David”; the title does not by itself settle the psalm’s history of composition.
The verb can mean trembling or being agitated, including anger.
“Alone” can emphasize the LORD as the sole giver of safety or the speaker lying down alone in safety.
vocabulary: Literally, sons of man; here an address to those dishonoring the speaker.

notes: Nehiloth is an uncertain musical term; it is often associated with wind instruments.
The speaker arranges something before God: the prayer is understood here, though arranging an offering is another possibility.
The hatred of evildoers is directed at people in the poem, not only at abstract wrongdoing.
Sheminith means something like “the eighth,” but its precise musical use is uncertain.
The speaker appeals to the absence of remembrance and praise in death. The lament is allowed its own voice without being rewritten into a complete teaching about the afterlife.
Shiggaion is an uncertain designation for the poem or its performance. The title refers to Cush the Benjaminite, whose circumstances are not explained here.
The difficult second clause can concern rescuing a causeless enemy or plundering an adversary.
The draft takes the one who does not turn back as the wicked person, followed by God preparing weapons. The sequence of subjects is not explicit.
vocabulary: A bodily image for inward motives and feelings.

sections.1: Your name in all the earth

notes: Gittith is an uncertain musical designation. The clause about placing glory above the heavens is grammatically difficult.
The pinned Hebrew says “strength”; “praise” belongs to another textual tradition used in a later quotation.
The Hebrew elohim can mean God or divine beings. The draft follows “God” while leaving the alternative visible here.
vocabulary: The paired expressions mortal and son of man describe human beings in their frailty.

notes: Muth-labben is an uncertain musical direction or title.
Psalms 9 and 10 share a partial alphabetic pattern in Hebrew. The English keeps their received division and does not force an artificial acrostic.
Higgaion may concern meditation or a musical sound; its precise function with Selah is uncertain.
The draft understands the disputed term as fear; it has also been read as teacher.
vocabulary: An image of holding bloodshed accountable.

sections.1: Why do you stand far away?

notes: The second clause can be a wish that the wicked be trapped, or a description of the poor being trapped.
The Hebrew uses bless in a difficult expression. It can function as a euphemism for cursing God; another reading describes blessing the greedy person.
The written and read forms are difficult. The line can describe the victim being crushed or the attacker crouching.
vocabulary: The wicked person’s inward stance in the poem.
A child without a father’s protection, paired here with those who have no other helper.

notes: The extent of the advisers’ quotation is editorially supplied; the Hebrew does not mark its ending. Verse 1 has different written and read forms for fleeing.
The pinned word is “snares,” although some translations read “coals.”
The final clause can mean that the upright see God’s face or that his face beholds the upright.
vocabulary: A vivid image of God examining human beings.

notes: Sheminith is an uncertain musical direction involving the eighth.
The last phrase can describe one longing for safety or one being puffed at or scorned.
The furnace and earth expression is difficult; the refining of silver remains clear.

The Hebrew moves between plural “them” and singular “him.” The immediate concern is protection amid a corrupt generation; the grammar should not be made into an unqualified claim about manuscript transmission.
vocabulary: Literally, a heart and a heart: divided or deceptive intention.

sections.1: How long will you forget me?

notes: The Hebrew title appears before the poem. The final two English verses form one verse in Hebrew.
vocabulary: An appeal for renewed life before the sleep of death.

notes: Fool describes a morally reckless stance in this poem, not a measure of intellectual ability.
“My people” introduces a voice whose speaker is not explicitly named.
The final expression can concern restoring fortunes or bringing back captivity.
vocabulary: To turn toward God in one’s conduct and understanding.

sections.1: Who may live in your tent?

notes: The oath is understood as one kept even at personal cost. The compressed wording can also be read as swearing to do harm.
The text names interest without adding the qualifier excessive.
vocabulary: The sanctuary pictured as the LORD’s dwelling.

notes: Miktam is an uncertain designation in the title. “Of David” can also mean “for David.”
The pointed opening is feminine singular, “you have said,” sometimes understood as self-address. “I say” conveys that reading; the form and relation of the following clauses remain difficult.
The holy ones can be faithful people in the land or divine beings; the wording and connection with verse 4 are disputed.
The verb can concern hastening after another god or paying a bride-price. Blood libations remain explicit.
The pinned text says “my glory”; it is not silently changed to tongue from a later quotation.
Pit can also be understood as decay. The identity and timing implied by the faithful one are not settled through a later interpretation.
vocabulary: The Hebrew bodily image for inward counsel.

notes: The final expression can describe a resolution about speech or a thought God does not find.
Closing their fat is an image of hardened or unfeeling hearts.
The draft follows the read “us”; the written form says “me.”

The description of worldly people, stored goods, children, and what is left over is difficult. It can picture their present abundance, or be heard as a wish that judgment reach them and their descendants.
The awakening is not explicitly dated or identified as resurrection.
vocabulary: An image of something closely guarded.

notes: The complete title connects the song with rescue from enemies and Saul. It precedes the opening confession in the Hebrew. Compare the related song in 2 Samuel 22; this draft follows the pinned Psalm rather than harmonizing its differences.
Hail and burning coals are repeated in the pinned text and retained.
The response to the crooked uses a verb of twisting or dealing shrewdly, not the same virtue named in the preceding lines.
The word translated “gentleness” can concern humility or condescension.
The king’s crushing and destroying of enemies is explicit military violence, not recast as a struggle against abstract faults.
The draft follows the read form, giving great victories, rather than treating the unpointed written form as a tower.
vocabulary: A horn symbolizes powerful protection or victory.
A heavenly creature associated with the divine presence.

notes: The draft reads the heavens’ testimony as wordless. Another understanding is that there is no speech or language where their voice is unheard.
The pinned word means line, often a measuring line. “Voice” or “sound” reflects a different reading familiar from another textual tradition.
The plural can concern presumptuous sins or arrogant people. The draft follows the former.
vocabulary: The spread-out sky in the poem’s ancient imagery.
One who acts to reclaim or deliver another.

notes: The prayer addresses one person, understood from the following verses as the king.
The Hebrew accents place a strong pause after “save.” Another familiar reading is “LORD, save the king; answer us when we call.”
vocabulary: An offering consumed on the altar.
The king consecrated for his role.

notes: The royal prayer speaks expansively of life forever and ever. The draft preserves the expression.
The addressee can be understood as God or as the king empowered by God. The text itself shifts to naming the LORD in verse 9.
The destruction of offspring is part of the poem’s severe vision of victory and is not softened.
vocabulary: Steadfast loyalty that sustains the king.

notes: “The Doe of the Dawn” appears to be a performance direction or tune title; its exact function is uncertain.
The phrase can picture God enthroned on Israel’s praises or dwelling among them.
The mockers’ taunt shifts from addressing the sufferer to speaking about him. The change is retained.

The pinned Hebrew reads “like a lion—my hands and feet,” with no expressed verb. Readings rendered “dug” or “pierced” belong to alternative textual interpretations or witnesses. The draft preserves the pinned wording and its difficulty instead of silently harmonizing a later application.
“You have answered me” is a completed-action form in the pinned text. Its abrupt appearance marks the turn toward praise.
The final clause is difficult and can mean that a person has not kept, or cannot keep, life alive. The draft understands it as mortal inability.
vocabulary: A region associated with rich pasture and powerful cattle.
A dry fragment of broken pottery.

notes: The word can mean deepest darkness or the shadow of death. The draft retains danger without restricting it to the moment of death.
The pointed verb means return; dwelling reflects another reading or understanding. “Length of days” is retained without deciding between a long life and an unlimited future.
vocabulary: Tools of the shepherd’s protection and guidance.
Goodness and faithful love pursue the speaker, reversing an image often used of enemies.

sections.1: The earth belongs to the LORD
sections.3: Who may stand in his holy place?

notes: The pinned text reads “my life,” an abrupt first-person form. Many translations follow “his life” from another reading; others connect the phrase with invoking God falsely. The draft keeps the received difficulty.
The read form is plural, “those who seek him.” “Jacob” may name the seeking people; “God of Jacob” is a familiar alternative that adds words not expressed in this pinned text.
vocabulary: An ancient image of the earth established over waters.
The LORD associated with heavenly armies or multitudes.
